Stated Claim / Post Context:
How popular is your - and your child's - name? Use our search tool to discover which 'middle-class' baby names are surging - and which Australian favourites are dying out

Once-common names are disappearing while a new wave of old-fashioned favourites linked to Australia's new middle class climbs the charts. Use our search tool to see where your name ranks.

Actual Article Body:
By SARAH BROOKES - SENIOR REPORTER, AUSTRALIA

Published:  23:59 AEDT, 21 October 2026   |  Updated:  00:01 AEDT, 22 October 2026

Australia's baby-name landscape has transformed, with once-dominant names such as Karen and Gary disappearing from the top 100 as vintage favourites roar back - and Muhammad climbs from 100th in 2013 to 38th in 2025.

The playground roll call is also taking an old-fashioned turn, with George, Arthur, Hazel and Florence enjoying remarkable revivals, while names synonymous with more recent generations, such as Kylie and Michael, fade away.

Oliver remains king of the boys' names, taking the number one spot for the 12th consecutive year in 2025, ahead of Noah and Theodore.

Charlotte has reclaimed the girls' crown from Isla, which topped the rankings in 2024, with Amelia holding onto second place and Isla slipping to third.

But some of the most dramatic changes become apparent when the rankings are viewed over decades rather than years.

Names once considered old-fashioned are being dusted off for a new generation, in part due to their perception as being 'middle class', with Daisy climbing from 90th in 2016 to 23rd in 2025, while Elsie has surged from 79th to 28th over the same period.

The revival isn't confined to girls. Henry has climbed from 19th in 2015 to fourth in 2025, while George has risen from 42nd to 21st over the same period.

Arthur's comeback has been similarly striking. After sitting outside the top 100 as recently as 2017, it entered at 84th in 2018 and has since surged to 19th.

Your browser does not support iframes.

Australia's baby-name landscape has transformed, with once-dominant names such as Karen and Gary disappearing from the top 100 as vintage favourites roar back. (Pictured: Schoolchildren knitting in a Sydney classroom in 1964)

Perhaps the starkest evidence of changing tastes, however, can be found in the names that have fallen out of fashion.

Many of the names that dominated the 1960s and 1970s, including Karen, Michelle, Michael and Peter, have disappeared from the top 100.

Joshua topped all four of the 1995 state lists examined, for South Australia, NSW, Western Australia and Queensland, but has fallen to 87th nationally in 2025.

Other boys' names synonymous with the 1990s have suffered similar fates. Matthew, Nicholas and Michael have disappeared from the current top 100 altogether, while Daniel has dropped to 79th and Benjamin to 50th.

For girls, Jessica's fall is even more dramatic. It occupied the top spot in all four of the 1995 state lists examined but does not appear in the 2025 national top 100.

Sarah, Rebecca, Stephanie and Amy have also vanished from the top 100, while Emma has fallen to 78th.

Muhammad has travelled in the opposite direction, climbing from 100th nationally in 2013 to 38th in 2025.

Meaning 'praiseworthy' in Arabic, the name has deep significance in Islam and is used widely across the Muslim world, with numerous variations including Mohammed, Mohammad and Mohamed.

Your browser does not support iframes.

But what makes one name suddenly desirable and another hopelessly dated can be about far more than fashion.

Monash University sociologist Jo Lindsay interviewed dozens of predominantly middle-class Australian parents for a study examining naming, social class and gender.

She argued a child's first name could function as a form of 'symbolic capital', helping locate the child socially, and found parents often considered how the name they chose might follow their son or daughter into adulthood.

For some, that meant imagining the name on a business card, in a boardroom or attached to a prestigious profession.

'There is more freedom for parents to choose first names for their children on the basis of individual taste as institutional, religious and extended family pressures decline,' she said.

'Australian boys are more likely than girls to be given traditional names. Boys are also more likely to be given a name shared by members of the British royal family, though these are popular for girls as well.'

In terms of girls' names, Charlotte has reclaimed the crown from Isla, which topped the rankings in 2024, with Amelia holding onto second place and Isla slipping to third. (Pictured: a stock image of Australian children at a school assembly)

Your browser does not support iframes.

Ms Lindsay said once a name catches on among high-income, highly educated parents, it starts working its way down the socio-economic ladder.

'In terms of social class, mothers' education has been found to have a strong influence on naming choices in the USA. This is particularly the case with naming girls,' she said.

'Parents are interested in aspirational names that sound 'successful', which reinforces a fashion cycle where upper-class parents choose relatively obscure names to distinguish their children and these are then taken on by lower-class families in the following decade.'

One mother interviewed for the Australian study explained why she had deliberately opted for a conventional choice.

Monash University sociologist Jo Lindsay (pictured) interviewed dozens of predominantly middle-class Australian parents for a study examining naming, social class and gender. She argued a child's first name could function as a form of 'symbolic capital', helping locate the child socially

'We wanted a traditional name and we also looked at something that's going to fit them when they're a child but is also going to fit them when they're 90.'

Another worried that her son's name could shape people's first impressions of him.

'People often have an idea of who a person is when they read their name on a business card.'

A lawyer who took part in the research described wanting names that would fit comfortably within the professional circles in which she worked, recalling that her partner thought one choice was 'a great judge's name'.

She wanted her children to have names carrying 'a bit of authority' and which would not seem out of place attached to a doctor, judge or other professional.

Yet parents also faced a dilemma: how to find something distinctive without saddling a child with a name that would stood out for the wrong reasons.

One participant wanted 'a fairly traditional name that was a little bit unique but without being really out there', while another deliberately avoided top-10 names after growing up with an extremely common name herself.

The research also exposed an uncomfortable degree of class snobbery surrounding baby names.

Some middle-class participants dismissed invented or creatively spelt names as 'bogan', describing them as 'checkout operator' or Centrelink-client names. Others derided what they saw as 'made-up' names with 'creative spelling' .

Your browser does not support iframes.

The quintessential fictional parody was Kath & Kim's spectacularly named Epponnee-Raelene Kathleen Darlene Charlene Craig, which several participants cited when discussing names they considered ridiculous.

One participant also singled out Poppy and Dakota as fashionable choices she believed could prove detrimental later in life.

'You can't see your child sitting on the bench at the High Court of Australia being called Poppy or something.'

Names incorporating numbers or Roman numerals, such as Kviiilyn (pronounced 'Kaitlyn', using V-I-I for eight), have turned up in local records.

Gold Coast mum Jessica Mavis, wrote into the Australian magazine That's Life in June 2016 explaining that she loved the name Kaitlyn but hated how popular it was. Her husband suggested replacing the 'ait' sound with the Roman numeral for eight (VIII).

Other unusual names on the birth registry include for boys Lucifer, Lazer, Lightning, Ocean-Stanley and Marvel while for girls there is Panda, Moet, Narnia-Jay, Nivea, and Ginkgo.

McCrindle social researcher Sophie Renton said the current top 100 offered a unique insight into how Australia's social and cultural fabric is changing.

'Muhammad has grown a lot over the last few years, which speaks to our cultural diversity as a nation,' she told Daily Mail Australia.

'And there has been a shift to a name becoming a personal brand in the era of social media.'

Ms Renton said baby names, like fashion, moved in cycles, but once stereotypes became attached to a name they could be difficult to shake.

'Fashion always repeats itself, and what we're seeing now is this resurgence back to some of those names that are associated with our great-grandparents,' she said.

But names associated with more recent generations can face a longer road back.

'As for the name Karen, anyone that was alive during that time has associations with the name Karen, which will likely be hard to shake for maybe the next 15 or 20 years until a new generation that hasn't had that experience have different associations with that name.'

Ms Renton said the search for individuality was one factor that could help turn an old-fashioned name into something desirable again.

'People are going, "Oh, I want to find a different name for my child," so they start exploring names that haven't been used for a while,' she said.

'And we are in our thrifting era, so people are really looking at the vintage world right now.'

But today's hottest names could eventually become victims of their own success.

As parents search for something more unique or different, they can begin looking beyond the top 10, she said.

Another change is the growing popularity of nicknames as official first names, with an increasing number of parents going straight to the shorter version.

The trend is evident in the 2025 rankings, where Charlie sits at number eight for boys, while Billy, Louie, Tommy and Alfie all make the top 100.

'Historically parents gave their child the option of the formal sounding name with the nickname, but we've just gone straight to the nickname now.'

She said the growing importance placed on children's names could also be seen through the lens of social media and personal branding.

'Social media maybe isn't the one sole driver - it's part of the changing societal fabric, which I think is putting more weight on names than there has been before.'

That raises an intriguing question for today's fastest-rising names: can newfound popularity eventually become the very thing that sends fashion-conscious parents searching for something new?

And with babies born from 2025 marking the beginning of a new generation - Generation Beta - names near the bottom of today's rankings could provide clues about what comes next.

Elodie and Lainey have entered the girls' top 100, while Margot, Lottie, Maeve and Remi are among the names to watch.

For boys, Julian, Maverick and Caleb are among the 2025 arrivals or returnees, while Theo, Ezra, Billy, Louie and Roman reflect the continuing appetite for short, distinctive names.

For now Oliver and Charlotte reign supreme. But as Karen, Jessica and Joshua demonstrate, no baby name stays fashionable forever.
